⏱️ ~22 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, there’s a reason I am most productive when working from an office, and it’s not the harsh lighting or lack of distractions: It’s my office chair.
  • It has been revealed that over the years that the Shop AD team has been testing office chairs, often corralling the entire office to take a seat, we’ve expanded our search to curate a high-low selection that includes wallet-friendly picks, but also household names in the ergonomic space, like Herman Miller and Knoll.
  • Our editors and writers have personally sat on, worked, and Zoomed from each of these picks, at the office and from their home desks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, there’s a reason I am most productive when working from an office, and it’s not the harsh lighting or lack of distractions: It’s my office chair. Previously, I was convinced that “ergonomic” was an empty buzzword used by chiropractors and human resources, but after working from a slew of supportive seats these last few years, I’m a believer. Ideally, office chairs combine a sophisticated aesthetic with a genuinely functional build—and both things can be true in the same design. Maybe that budget mesh chair you picked up from an office supply store does the job, but is it the right culture fit for the very curated aesthetic of your home? Fortunately, I’ve sourced the products that check all the boxes, because you deserve to feel just as productive in your guest room-slash-office space.

It has been revealed that over the years that the Shop AD team has been testing office chairs, often corralling the entire office to take a seat, we’ve expanded our search to curate a high-low selection that includes wallet-friendly picks, but also household names in the ergonomic space, like Herman Miller and Knoll. Our favorite options cosigned by design lovers—we are Architectural Digest after all—and those looking to cure that stubborn tech neck twinge, finally.

Our editors and writers have personally sat on, worked, and Zoomed from each of these picks, at the office and from their home desks. We can attest that not only are they attractive, but they will also provide structural support for your entire body, even through the longest meeting days and tightest deadlines.

As a general practice, the armrests on ergonomic office chairs tend to be bulky. Not so with the Branch Verve Chair, which stands out with its curvy S-shaped supports that give it some space-y, extraterrestrial appeal. The Verve is a newer and sportier model from the brand that set out to modernize dated office furniture (from standing desks to seating), and boasts a sleek breathable mesh back and some slender legs with casters for wheeling around the office.

Contributor Terri Williams notes that sitting for long periods of time is easy thanks to the V-shaped chair design that provides extra lumbar support. At just a hair shy of $600, this chair is also one of the most affordable picks on the list (so it’s a good fit for most people), and one of the most streamlined if you hate the look of typical corporate chairs. The svelte design is why we chose it as our top pick over the AD editor-beloved Ergonomic Chair Pro below, which might not be as visually appealing to the average person. “I can also adjust the height of the softly-padded armrests, the seat depth, the tilt, the tilt tension, and the padded lumbar support,” Williams says of the extra features here that put it into holy grail territory.

According to recent reports, there’s a reason the Aeron is Herman Miller’s most beloved and recognizable office chair. The iconic design is truly supportive and customizable to fit your ideal comfort zones, with adjustable offerings from the armrests to the seat itself. The seat is almost bouncy, springing you upright and into the most ergonomic position possible. In her other office chair, shopping editor Audrey Lee sits on a cushion, but states that the Aeron balances support with real comfort. Contributor Zoë Sessums selected hers after a virtual fitting with an ergonomic expert at Herman Miller, who walked her through all the features. (Herman Miller offers an informative online gallery of both imagery and detailed videos if you’re unable to try out a chair in person.) Once the chair was delivered—no assembly required, it literally rolls out of the box—Sessums came away impressed with the power of the patented PostureFit SL back support, which encourages opening up the chest and shoulders, and tilts the pelvis slightly forward. “This chair will save your body,” she notes. “It’s easy to see why people invest in supreme desk setups. I would recommend the Aeron chair again and again.”.

Sources indicate that A bad case of tech neck hates to see the Branch Ergo Pro coming. That’s because the chair’s fully customizable support system is calibrated to ensure that your posture is optimized, even during long hours in one fixed position. It offers 14 points of adjustments total (count ’em!) to keep you comfortable, from the seat height to the headrest for those who are blessed with longer limbs. And compared to the original version reviewed above, this one is far cushier on the seat and armrests, with seven additional points of adjustability. It is slightly less svelte and also slightly more expensive than its predecessor, the original Branch Ergonomic, which our tester Williams also loved for its ergonomic design.

Each of our editors took a spin on the Branch Ergo Pro (read our full review) and came away smitten with the adjustability points and glutes support of this “double-stuffed” chair. “I was especially fond of the arm rests that helped me achieve perfect elbow support with my laptop stand and that the adjustable tilt option gave me the freedom to stretch my back out whenever needed,” commerce editor Audrey Lee noted.

The only drawback is that the Ergo Pro needs assembly out of the box, and the construction process is a bit of a learning curve. Still, everything came together swiftly in about 30 minutes or less and was easy enough to complete solo. Since it can be fully disassembled, it’s also a great option for frequent movers.

It has been revealed that there’s a lot to like about Haworth’s Breck chair. Lee reported that it arrived swiftly in a large box that was simple to carry inside. The assembly won’t leave you frustrated either. You’ll find instructions on the flaps of the delivery box and Haworth has the same manual available on their website as well as a short video with step-by-step directions. The whole process literally takes less than a couple of minutes before you’re ready to put the chair in action.

Don’t be fooled by the easy assembly process, though, as this office chair is more advanced than meets the eye. “I first received the Breck during a heat wave and appreciated the ultra-breathable backrest which allowed a comfortable amount of air to flow through,” claims Lee. But it’s all the adjustable features that stand out to her. Need more tilt? No problem. Wish the armrests were just a tad longer? Easy. Height? Seat depth? Lumbar support? Done, done, and done. And while these are all perks you would expect from a high-priced chair that costs over $1,000, the Breck supplies them at under $500.

A high price tag comes with great expectations—which the Asari chair met completely. Lee appreciated its attention to detail, which included the soft leather, the perfect amount of foam fill in the seat, and a backrest that makes it a treat to sit down and work. “The chair has noticeably softened in a delightful way that’s ultra-accommodating to my dimensions without feeling too sunken in or too stiff,” she states. Unlike leather executive office chairs that can read harsh or overly corporate, the Asari’s look is unparalleled. Lee “absolutely recommends” this chair to anyone looking to splurge on their home office. From physical appearance to practical use, it scores 10s across the board.

Industry observers note that it’s rare for a truly ergonomic chair to look as good as the Herman Miller Management Chair does. I chose the brown checkerboard upholstery and stainless steel frame and, not to brag, but my coworkers have since declared FOMO, requesting fun office chairs of their own. Like most Herman Miller options, this chair is very adjustable—the features I focused on customizing to my liking were the seat height and the amount of recline the back can have (which is a lot, actually, I feel like I’m lying down if I push too hard). The back cushion has a bit more firmness to it than the ultra-plush seat cushion, which is great for posture correction and staying focused. While it’s a bit too soft for my all-day liking, I do appreciate the additional padding on days when I know I’ll be mostly stationary. I rarely need to adjust my position, and my knees never fall asleep, something that used to happen quite often in my too-tall office chair. Overall, the management chair is excellent for both a home and office environment. With over a dozen upholstery options, you won’t have to worry about the seat clashing with your existing decor—I find it a stylish midcentury alternative to the often all-black silhouettes that plague traditional offices.

For anyone in need of a custom office chair, Steelcase has solutions. Senior commerce editor Nashia Baker settled on this grey leather version from 23 upholstery options, which allow you to choose from peachy pinks, neutrals, and warm leather hues. The overall silhouette is narrower than most, but the armrests are adjustable and the seat has a soft, gentle glide when maneuvered up or down. Even the wheels are smooth when rolling over floors, carpet or tile. “This chair has literally made the trek with me across the Condé Nast office and on various floors, though I haven’t noticed the wheels wearing or jamming in the months I’ve been testing it,” Baker notes. With its stable, upright backrest, the seat discourages slouching, but also has enough give for comfortably sitting hour after hour. At over $2,000, it’s definitely an investment, but for all the custom flourishes, Baker says it’s all worth it.

For those in search of a no frills office chair, this West Elm one is sleek and simple. This is the least adaptable option on this list, in that it doesn’t allow for any other heights or tilts. What it lacks in ergonomic adjustment points, however, it makes up for in design prowess. The sleek stainless steel frame and leather seat make a more eye-catching pair, while the true-ball wheels roll smoothly and without catching on the carpet in the AD office. This is definitely for those who prefer a firmer seat and I liked how upright this office chair felt, like it was almost correcting my posture while encouraging a better sense of productivity. My colleague, shopping editor Audrey Lee, however, wasn’t a fan, stating that it was too firm and didn’t love that the seat doesn’t swivel. “It’s a beautiful chair, and looks much more expensive than the price suggests,” Lee says. “It’s a divisive option, but the straightforward make is something I’d prefer to have at home, when all of my distractions are nearby, and I need the chair to do the heavy-lifting of forcing me to lock in.”.

Recent findings suggest that branch’s Softside chair is a fully upholstered take on their more technical office chairs. It’s still as intuitively designed as the brand’s other chairs with its adjustment points (removable arms, adjustable height, and tension recline), two back heights, and caster wheels, but think of this as your at-home companion to the Ergonomic Pro. Brighter upholstery—I’m partial to the skylight blue—also helps to cheer up a workspace suffering from too much black and grey.

The iconic Danish brand HAY has made a number of noteworthy pieces, but we’re drawn to this amply cushioned roller chair. Dating back to 2009, the 155 Task Chair has two styles: standard and soft. The latter has foam padding and batting that keeps you supported through hours-long meetings. At 20 pounds, it’s a relatively lightweight item, and it conveniently arrives fully assembled for a fuss-free setup process. Plus, the curved seat is one of several ergonomic elements. The chair has a tilting mechanism and gas lift to adjust the angle and height of the seat. This is one of many chairs in HAY’s best-selling About a Chair collection, developed by award-winning furniture designer Hee Welling.

Introduced in 2021, the Zeph Chair is a collaboration between Herman Miller and Berlin-based design firm Studio 7.5. It also went on to earn one of AD’s 2022 Cleverest Awards, with editors noting its midcentury-modern design and ergonomic form for lower back support. The kinematic mono-shell is the most striking feature, a contoured seat and back with voids for a futuristic look. “Even better, the playful chair’s seat is made of 50% post-consumer recycled content and zero fabric waste,” adds Sessums. If you anticipate spending hours upon hours in this chair, we recommend the optional seat pad and arm rests for added comfort. Another thing to feel good about? The polymer shell is easy to clean with a damp cloth, and the 12-year warranty gives you extra peace of mind about investing in a relatively splurge-y item.

Sources indicate that louisa Pierce and Emily Ward of AD100 firm Pierce & Ward have been trusted to design homes for celebrity clients like Dakota Johnson and Emma Roberts, and their collaboration with West Elm indicates their vintage-inspired, quiet luxury aesthetic. This button-tufted, swiveling office chair will instantly ground your space. It’s sophisticated and substantial, and the adjustable height lever is located under the seat. If the in-stock upholstery isn’t for you, there are 74 options to customize your chair. So, if you’re working from your living room or the office, you should feel right at home—a concept Pierce and Ward considered while designing their firm’s new Los Angeles studio. As Ward previously shared with AD, “There’s just a different kind of energy when a workspace feels like a home.” Keep in mind this is a limited-edition product, so it’s best to nab it ASAP.

Recent findings suggest that one of the newest models from Swiss furniture manufacturer Vitra, the Mynt Task Chair is a thoughtfully designed, minimalist option for a modern office. Because of the slim profile, this would work well in a home office with a versatile, space-saving desk like the Pierce Wall Desk from West Elm. The natural oak veneer backrest, armrest, and seat is our preferred colorway, but the upholstered styles provide more cushioning, thanks to the polyurethane foam and polyester fiber fill. The responsive design adjusts the seat based on your movements (a.k.a. no manual adjustments needed), and the patented tilt mechanism is hidden within the aluminum frame. Pair it with an oak-stained desk to complement your chair, while also bringing more natural texture to a home office setup.

Industry observers note that for the midcentury aesthetes, Arhaus’s leather pieces are contemporary takes on nostalgic silhouettes. Case in point: the Kirsten Faux Leather Desk Chair, an ergonomic approach to a classic leather seat, complete with rounded edges. It can easily find a home in an earth-toned office with a walnut-stained desk, and the antique brass legs add another natural hue to the design. And while it may look like it hails from a different era, there are plenty of updated features, such as the hydraulic lift to change up the height of the seat. Four sturdy, powdercoated aluminum legs are designed to endure long days at the office. And if you’re drawn to the shape of curved back and seat, the brand’s Kirsten collection includes dining chairs and stools. We like the faux leather upholstery, but Arhaus also makes this office chair with green performance velvet and white textured performance weave if you want try other options.

Recent findings suggest that our commitment to bringing you quality seat recs is well documented, and finding an office chair that is comfortable, well-made, and easy on the eyes can make a world of difference in how you feel while you’re sitting in a seemingly endless one-hour meeting. The Shop AD team thoroughly vets items before including them in our roundups, and we test nearly everything we write about—office chairs being no exception. I, alongside our broader team of writers and editors, tested more than 30 chairs combined to pull together these rankings, with only a few making the cut in our best-of list. I’ve yet to find a stylish, non-bulky gaming chair that meets our standard, and several other generic Amazon picks just didn’t feel elevated enough to make our list of chairs that would suit a design lover—though they may tick the boxes from a purely practical standpoint. Our reviews are always thorough, in-depth, and honest, even when we’re noting how a chair may have fallen short.

Weary workers can rest assured that every pick on this list has been hand-picked and personally vetted by us. Our well-rounded list includes design head-approved picks (Herman Miller! Knoll! Steelcase!) with more approachable best-sellers on Amazon (like Branch) sprinkled in, with top priority going to picks that had a warranty of at least seven years and merged great design with adjustability and comfort.

Over the years spent testing, we’ve also delisted picks from Article, Haworth, Herman Miller, Flash Furniture, Steelcase, Flexispot, and Humanscale that either felt not ergonomic enough for an office setting or didn’t feel like the most superlative choice for their price bracket compared to their peers. The Article Svelti is armless, for example, while the Steelcase Gesture had a stiff backrest and a tedious assembly process. An older version of the Branch Ergonomic has been replaced with the brand new Branch Ergonomic Pro, which was tested by several of our editors.

Whether from the desks of the Condé Nast offices or from home setups, the Architectural Digest team has spent weeks (sometimes months or years) sitting in, working from, and recording their thoughts on the best office chairs. I am a firm believer that the chair makes the workplace, and my fellow editors agree, assuring that each of these chairs met a specific set of criteria—which I’ve outlined below—in order to pass the qualifications to be included in this article.

Recent findings suggest that delivery and assembly: Straight out the gate, did the chair arrive within the guaranteed delivery window? And if you had to assemble it, was it relatively easy to do so or did it come with a tough-to-parse manual and 100 parts?

Dimensions: Apartment dwellers know better than anyone that being conservative with floor real estate isn’t a want, but a need. That’s why our reviews provide exact measurements for the styles we tested and any notes on whether we thought a chair might not be a good fit (literally) for a modest-sized workspace.

Industry observers note that rating the experience: A chair that’s both easy on the eyes and on the tush is our number one priority. What was your first impression of the chair? Does the design fit a clear aesthetic? Is it meant to be ergonomic? How do the materials perform, and do they seem durable? How did you feel after a full work day and week? Does it include any fun details that may not be obvious at first glance? Our reviews were crafted to give insight on why a chair could be the right one for your 40-hour work week.

What to keep in mind: Everyone has different ideas of perfection—which is why each chair also has a section detailing what a potential buyer should keep in mind. For example, if assembly was particularly difficult, if the chair had special care instructions, and if the design seemed polarizing, we made note of all that.

Editor’s Note: We recently de-listed the Article Svelti office chair due to it being armless in favor of more supportive options.

What Features Should I Look for in an Office Chair?

Our experts—TikTok’s favorite neurosurgeon, Betsy Grunch, MD, FAANS, FACS and Gainesville Physical Therapy's Kristy Basinger PT, CHT—agree that your back rest should be made from breathable material such as mesh for better air circulation, decreased perspiration, and greater comfort overall. Your seat is another notable component for gluteal support that should have adequate padding consisting of dense foam or similar materials. Adjustability for different body types is crucial no matter which upcoming chair you choose, so you can ensure your feet are positioned flat on the floor and arms set at a 90-degree angle.

Why Are Office Chairs So Expensive?

Like any investment piece of furniture, you get what you pay for. There’s a lot of science that goes into crafting a comfortable and supportive office chair that you can actually be productive in. Ergonomic design, smooth movement, textiles, and manufacturing costs all combine to set the price point. Office chairs are so expensive because you’re not only investing in a chair, but also making an investment in your physical health. We spend at least eight hours a day in these seats, and they can dramatically affect our posture, joint health, and mobility. You may not notice the benefits of a great office chair, but you’ll definitely remember your discomfort in a bad one. Of course, there are budget-friendly options, like the Haworth Breck chair that we tested, which comes in above $400.

How Long do Office Chairs Typically Last?

Recent findings suggest that high-quality office chairs typically last between seven and 10 years, which is why we prioritized picks that offer a lengthy warranty to cover the majority of this period. Cheaper office chairs have a much shorter lifespan, typically just a few years. Non-performance fabrics and leather seats will show their age more than performance materials that are better equipped to handle stains, scratches, and general wear and tear. You’ll know it’s time for a new seat when the customizable features—such as armrests, height, and seat position—start to wear out and aren’t as easy to adjust.

What Are the Differences Between Office Chair Styles?

In a recent development, task: As the name suggests, task chairs are designed for specific tasks. Think of these chairs as short-term, minimal seating for quick bursts of work. They often have a less padded, simpler design and less support than true ergonomic office chairs that are designed for full days. Branch describes these seats as, “Task chairs embrace simplicity in their design, often characterized by a streamlined appearance. They prioritize functionality over excess features, aiming to deliver a no-frills seating solution that's easy to maneuver and adjust.” In this list, the Fritz Hansen Series 7 chair is a high-design task chair.

According to recent reports, executive: An executive office chair typically features a plush seat, high back, and ample spine support to keep you comfortable throughout the entire workday. You’ll find that these chairs offer more adjustment points and customization, like the 14 points on the Branch Ergonomic Pro we tested. Executive chairs come in a variety of materials and silhouettes, from Herman Miller’s signature Eames Aluminum Group chair to the brand’s more futuristic Aeron chair.

Gaming: The most specific type of office chair, gaming chairs have a very distinct shape. Usually with wide shoulders and an ultra-high back that supports your head and neck, gaming chairs prioritize lounge-style comfort without sacrificing ergonomic support. Most include a neck pillow and a lumbar pillow for additional padding and support. While the back is not as adjustable as some office chairs, gaming chairs offer additional customization points on the armrests and base.

What Office Furniture Does AD Recommend?

It has been revealed that your office chair is just a piece of the puzzle when it comes to outfitting your WFH setup. Brands like Herman Miller, Steelcase, and Branch all offer great desks, filing cabinets, and bookcases to help fill your workspace with design-minded pieces. For those who value flexibility and ergonomic support, look to Branch for our top-tested seats and sit-to-stand desks that can withstand all-day, everyday use. For the midcentury obsessed, there’s no better place to find retro pieces than Design Within Reach. Essential brands like Eames, Knoll, and Vipp are all featured alongside some more modern favorites like Audo Copenhagen, HAY, and Tom Dixon. While we may not be able to channel the Scandinavian vacation policies, we can infuse our workspaces with more of their colorful minimalism to combat that three o’clock slump. If you prefer something more sculptural than corporate-leaning, Lulu and Georgia offers curved stone desks, upholstered seats, and plenty of desk accessories to incorporate more personality. For a full rundown of where to buy office furniture, read our guide here.

Where Do Designers Buy Office Furniture?

In a recent development, across our vast library of home tours, we’ve noticed a few recurring characters for home offices that designers reach for again and again. Herman Miller, a favorite of our team as well, appears countless times. The retailer, having reached midcentury-modern icon status, is almost instantly recognizable. The aluminum frames, channeled leather upholstery, and wooden details elevate a home office while still providing tested ergonomic support. Jeff Goldblum’s California home boasts the brand’s Eames Aluminum Group chair, and Kevin Hart’s West Hollywood office features the Eames Executive Chair. Design Within Reach is another retailer designers frequent. Other midcentury staples can be found here too, like Knoll’s Morrison chair, the Vipp453+ Swivel Chair (which we’ve previously tested, but removed in favor of office chairs with more ergonomic features), and the Saarinen swivel chair (as seen in Margot Robbie’s production offices).

Does My Office Chair Need Lumbar Support?

Whether you’re sitting in your office chair eight hours a day or just here and there, yes, you need lumbar support. We’re all familiar with the aches that come when sleeping on a sofa for the night or after a long-haul flight, and proper back support helps to mitigate that pain and protect your spine in the process. According to our experts (Betsy Grunch, MD, FAANS, FACS and Gainesville Physical Therapy's Kristy Basinger PT, CHT, cited above), a proper-fitting desk chair is one of the cornerstones of postural health. People who sit for long hours in a poorly adjusted chair will experience neck, back, shoulder, and hip pain. This can trigger headaches, lack of concentration, and compression of the discs in the spine. Low back pain is one of the main reasons for missed days at work, so it’s essential to choose a chair that supports the spine. (It’s also not a bad idea to support your overall health and quality rest with a good mattress for back pain.).

Tesla unveils 7.4 MW Powercore to take on ex-exec Baglino’s Heron Link

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that tesla has unveiled Powercore, a solid-state medium-voltage transformer that also handles the inverter and breaker functions in a single unit.
  • It has been revealed that it’s made in America and scheduled to start operating in 2027.
  • Recent findings suggest that upgrade: Tesla has since released a full spec sheet for Powercore, including efficiency, warranty, and its data center prepares.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that tesla has unveiled Powercore, a solid-state medium-voltage transformer that also handles the inverter and breaker functions in a single unit. Tesla rates it at 7.4 MW (9 MVA) continuously at 34.5 kV, with grid-forming support up to 10 MVA of peak power.

It has been revealed that it’s made in America and scheduled to start operating in 2027. That’s the same year Heron Power, the startup founded by Tesla’s former top engineer Drew Baglino, plans to start volume production of its own solid-state transformer, the Heron Link.

Recent findings suggest that upgrade: Tesla has since released a full spec sheet for Powercore, including efficiency, warranty, and its data center prepares. We’ve updated the article with the newly introduced details.

In a recent development, tesla first stated it would build its own transformers in September 2025, when it unveiled Megapack 3 and Megablock. Megablock connects four Megapack 3 units to a transformer and switchgear, but Tesla shared next to nothing about the transformer itself.

Powercore is that missing piece. Tesla announced it today through its Tesla Megapack account on X:.

Sources indicate that introducing PowercoreSolid state medium voltage transformer, inverter and breaker – reliable, safe and secure7.4 MW/9 MVA continuously at 34.5 kVac w/ grid-forming support for 10MVA of peak powerMade in America. Operating 2027 pic.twitter.com/sHxqnpWJrf.

About an hour later, Tesla followed up with a much longer post on X laying out the full spec sheet:.

It also packs a built-in solid-state medium-voltage breaker that Tesla states clears faults up to 1,000x faster than a conventional breaker. There’s no flammable oil, and it’s modular, so components can be serviced in the field without swapping the whole unit.

It has been revealed that tesla is pitching one product for three markets: battery storage, utility-scale solar, and 800 Vdc data centers. For Megablock, Powercore replaces the current two-step setup, where Megapack’s inverters output 480 V AC before a separate transformer steps it up to medium voltage. Tesla says that old architecture had twice the losses. For solar, Powercore works as a central inverter for today’s 1,500 Vdc arrays and upcoming 2,000 Vdc systems.

Sources indicate that tesla still hasn’t shared pricing, customers, or a factory location. It only indicates Powercore will be made in the US “of U.S. and imported parts” with first units operating in 2027.

According to recent reports, the idea behind a solid-state transformer is simple enough. A typical solar or battery project uses low-voltage inverters to convert DC into AC, then a significant oil-filled, iron-core transformer to step that up to grid voltage. A solid-state unit does both jobs with silicon carbide power electronics, which means less gear, a smaller footprint, and active control over voltage and frequency. That control is what “grid-forming” means: the unit can help hold the grid steady instead of just following it.

And with lead times on conventional transformers stretching into years as data centers and renewable projects pile into interconnection queues, there’s real demand for an alternative.

You can’t look at Powercore without thinking of Heron Power.

Sources indicate that baglino spent 18 years at Tesla and finished as SVP of powertrain and energy, in charge of batteries, motors, power electronics, and energy products. He left in April 2024 and rolled out Heron Power in 2025 to build solid-state transformers.

According to recent reports, he brought a lot of Tesla’s power electronics talent with him. As we reported when Tesla first announced its transformer intends, Heron hired engineers who led power electronics design for Powerwall 3, the next-gen Megapack, and Superchargers, along with the person who ran Tesla’s power electronics controls team for charging and energy products.

Since then, Heron has raised a $38 million Series A, a $140 million Series B led by Andreessen Horowitz and Breakthrough Energy Ventures, and a $60 million credit facility from J.P. Morgan and TriplePoint Capital. Former Tesla CFO Zach Kirkhorn sits on its board, and Tesla co-founder JB Straubel is an investor.

It’s also building Heron Factory One, a 286,000-square-foot plant in Morgan Hill, California, designed to make 10,000 Heron Links a year. That’s over 40 GW of annual capacity, with commercial production planned for late 2027.

And the customers are lining up. Vantage reserved more than 1 GW for its data centers, Intersect reserved 1.5 GW, LG Energy Solution Vertech is integrating Heron Link with its US-made battery systems, and RWE signed a pilot to install Heron Links at a Texas battery storage site in April 2027. Baglino says Heron has 50 GW of orders in the pipeline.

Here’s how the two compare based on what each company has disclosed:.

According to recent reports, on paper, Powercore is the bigger box, and now it has the better numbers too. At 7.4 MW continuous, it carries about 50% more power per unit than the 5 MW Heron Link, and its 98.86% peak efficiency edges out Heron’s 98.6%. But Tesla’s figure is a peak number, and Heron doesn’t label its own as one, so it’s not quite apples to apples. Neither organization has shared pricing.

Tesla is also going straight at Heron’s data center pitch. Powercore converts medium voltage directly to 800 Vdc, the rack architecture Nvidia is pushing, and Tesla says it’s working with Nvidia on 800 Vdc designs. Heron’s data center version does the same 34.5 kV AC to 800 VDC conversion with built-in storage, and data centers make up about a third of its business. Tesla’s answer to the storage piece is Megapack on the DC bus, and it says it already has 10 GWh of Megapack running at data centers.

This one is a little awkward for Tesla.

Recent findings suggest that A massive chunk of the people who designed Tesla’s power electronics over the last decade now work at Heron, and the guy who ran the whole org is its CEO. Tesla’s energy business also lost its longtime leader, Mike Snyder, last month, according to the WSJ.

This is all wrong. Tesla started developing this 3 years ago. Before Heron. The team selling Powercore is same as Megapack that has a way larger customer base than Heron. Also Heron is not a bankable company per project finance terms. So they will struggle to get projects financed through equity and senior debt . Not as Tesla.

According to recent reports, to be fair, Tesla still has plenty of power electronics expertise. Its silicon carbide inverters are in millions of cars and every Megapack. And it has something Heron doesn’t: a massive installed base and a sales channel. Tesla says it’s almost sold out of Megapacks for 2027, and bundling Powercore into Megablock is an easy upsell. Plenty of developers will take the one-stop shop.

Tesla’s specs now match or beat Heron’s on paper. But Heron has named customers, a pilot site with an install date, and a factory under construction. Tesla has none of those yet. I wouldn’t be surprised if Heron is actually ahead here.

But either way, the transformer shortage is big enough for both companies to sell everything they can build.

As data centers and fresh solar and battery projects pile onto the grid, utilities are scrambling for equipment and passing those costs on to ratepayers. Potatoes grown in moon dirt are as nutritious as Earth potatoes

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that astronauts living in the first permanent lunar base may see a sizable number of spuds on their dinner plates.
  • “We found that potatoes can complete their entire life cycle in simulated lunar soil when supplemented with organic matter,” Aymeric Goyer, an OSU botanist and study co-author, said in a statement.
  • Even in a controlled habitat, life on the moon will be physically demanding for astronauts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that astronauts living in the first permanent lunar base may see a sizable number of spuds on their dinner plates. In a study published today in the journal npj Microgravity, botanists at Oregon State University (OSU) proved it’s possible to grow healthy, edible potatoes in simulated moon soil with the help of everyday worms. Importantly, the team also identified the proper proportions of lunar regolith and compost needed to produce potato yields similar to those grown on Earth.

“We found that potatoes can complete their entire life cycle in simulated lunar soil when supplemented with organic matter,” Aymeric Goyer, an OSU botanist and study co-author, said in a statement. “That’s an important step toward developing reliable food production systems that could support long-term human exploration of the Moon.”.

Even in a controlled habitat, life on the moon will be physically demanding for astronauts. They’ll require carefully maintained, nutritious diets to keep them healthy, but it’s not as simple as sending them off packed with calorically dense prepackaged meals. Cargo room on spacecraft is limited and costly, and the desolate lunar surface isn’t exactly hospitable to agriculture. In addition to constant bombardment by cosmic and solar radiation, temperatures can swing anywhere between 250 degrees and -410 degrees Fahrenheit.

Recent findings suggest that indoor horticulture will also be challenging. Lunar regolith is an annoyingly powdery substance composed of sharp-edged, miniscule particles created over billions of years of asteroid impacts, but little else. With essentially no organic material at all, the dust alone isn’t capable of supporting plant life.

Recent findings suggest that while it is easy enough to combine that lunar regolith with agricultural additives, researchers weren’t sure if these could overcome moon soil’s heavy metals and irradiation. To test it, Goyer and his colleagues first obtained simulated lunar regolith made to resemble the samples collected during the Apollo missions. Regolith composition varies by region on the moon, so they selected five different types based on darker lunar mare dust and the lighter lunar highland soil. They then mixed the mock moon dust with vermicompost, the nutrient-rich soil created when worms break down organic materials. Next, they planted potatoes in various ratios of regolith and vermicompost, and monitored their growth. As a control, the team even planted potatoes in soil taken from Hermiston, Oregon, an area famous for some of the world’s highest spud yields.

Industry observers note that the team found that composite soil with only 30 percent vermicompost was enough to produce potato crops comparable to those farmed on Earth. Their findings suggest the supplemental organics bind to the regolith’s heavy metals, which shield the plants and minimize any damage to their roots.

“We believe the compost helps balance some of the toxicity we see in lunar regolith,” added OSU botanist and study co-author David Handy.

Sources indicate that but bushels of moon potatoes only go so far if they lack any real nutritional value. Even here, the lunar simulations offered promising results, particularly when it came to glycoalkaloids. The naturally forming potato toxins can cause green skin discoloration, but analysis indicated no statistically relevant rise in glycoalkaloids for the lunar crops.

With the potato viability debate settled, Goyer’s team will next compare 10 specific spud varieties grown in simulated lunar regolith to determine the most nutritious and resilient options for NASA astronomers.

  • BMW officially opened its new Plant Woodruff in South Carolina on November 13, marking the start of series production of its sixth-generation (Gen6) electric vehicle batteries.
  • The Gen6 batteries will power BMW’s upcoming “X” electric vehicles, starting with the all-new iX5 SUV.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The iX5 is BMW’s first fully electric vehicle built in the US, promising an estimated up to 456 miles of range, ultra-fast charging speeds, and plenty of Neue Klasse tech.

BMW officially opened its new Plant Woodruff in South Carolina on November 13, marking the start of series production of its sixth-generation (Gen6) electric vehicle batteries.

The Gen6 batteries will power BMW’s upcoming “X” electric vehicles, starting with the all-new iX5 SUV.

The iX5 is being built about 15 miles away at BMW Group Plant Spartanburg, the organization’s first fully electric model to be assembled in the US.

BMW Plant Spartanburg is churning out around 70 iX5s a day following a $1.7 billion investment in South Carolina to expand the plant for EV production and build the fresh battery assembly plant in Woodruff.

According to Robert Engelhorn, president and CEO of BMW Manufacturing in Spartanburg, the organization is confident the iX5 will attract buyers, promising 435 miles of range, ultra-fast charging, and its updated Neue Klasse technology and design.

Engelhorn told Automotive News in an interview that “there’s a clear trend globally for EVs,” adding that “We will contribute to this growth from the BMW side.”.

BMW didn’t provide a specific production estimate for the iX5, but suppliers were reportedly told it would be around 60,000 EVs in 2027, down from 100,000 it initially forecasted.

“We said we would begin assembling fully electric BMW vehicles in the US by the end of 2026 – and we are delivering on that commitment,” Engelhorn said.

A tech giant spokesperson confirmed that the iX5 will initially use battery cells from China before switching to US-sourced cells from LG Energy Solutions plant in Arizona by the end of the decade.

With production now underway, the iX5 is expected to begin arriving at US dealerships in early 2027.

In a recent development, the 2027 BMW iX5 60 xDrive starts at $79,800. BMW estimates the 144 kWh battery will provide up to 456 miles of range, up from the 435 miles it previously estimated.

Sources indicate that it features BMW’s new “double-X” light signature, which combines the headlights, daytime running lights, side lights, and turn signals into one unit. The Double-X headlights come standard, but BMW noted you can switch them for simpler diagonal stripes.

Last month, BMW showcased the i5’s ultra-fast-charging capabilities during a media event in Southern California with IONNA and Alpitronic.

During the demo, the iX5 60 xDrive hit a peak of 464 kW, which BMW said enables it to add an impressive up to 170 miles of range in 10 minutes.

The electric SUV features a dual-motor all-wheel-drive powertrain setup that delivers a combined 578 hp (425 kW) and 593 lb-ft of torque. BMW notes it can go from 0 to 60 mph in 4.4 seconds and tow up to 6,000 lbs.

Inside, the iX5 adopts BMW’s Neue Klasse design and tech, like the smaller iX3 SUV. The setup includes a new 17.9″ infotainment touchscreen and BMW’s Panoramic Vision, which spans the bottom of the windshield. There’s also an optional 14.6″ passenger screen for a third display.

Industry observers note that this is at the top of our short list. Out of Spec got 411 miles at 70 mph (by contrast the Gravity rated at 450 got 368 on the same run and the R1S rated at 410 got 349). It is a real 400+ mile vehicle with an ability to charge a real 300 miles in ~20 minutes.

Sources indicate that edit: OOS was with 22" wheels rated at 426. It should get >430 with the standard 21" wheels.

Measuring 197.2″ long, 78.7″ wide, and 68.9″ tall, BMW’s new iX5 is about the size of the Porsche Cayenne Electric.

Industry observers note that by 2030, BMW plans to be assembling at least fully electric models at Plant Spartanburg. “This marks the beginning of the next chapter in the success story of the largest plant in our global production network,” Raymond Wittman, BMW’s head of production, stated.

Following Debrecen (Hungary), Irlbach-Straßkirchen (Germany), and Shenyang (China), Woodruff is the fourth site in BMW’s production network to begin series production of the Gen6 batteries.

#168556. Industry News: Should Scientists Ignore Philosophers of Science?

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Should Scientists Ignore Philosophers of Science?

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (943 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 26, 2026 | Reviewed by Kaja Perina.
  • The eminent evolutionary biologist and modeller John Maynard Smith was once asked about Karl Popper and the philosophy of science.
  • Industry observers note that this is why I've recently published an academic article on the topic.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 26, 2026 | Reviewed by Kaja Perina.

The eminent evolutionary biologist and modeller John Maynard Smith was once asked about Karl Popper and the philosophy of science. His answer was not flattering. His impression was that scientists who take the philosophy of science seriously, and allow their research to be influenced by philosophical preconceptions, are "far more likely to do themselves harm than good". He loved reading philosophy of science and was always ready to argue about it, he added, but he did not believe that one should allow oneself to be influenced by it when actually thinking about science.

Industry observers note that this is why I've recently published an academic article on the topic. These are quite radical words, and though Maynard Smith's generalisation is untenable, there is an important insight to be extracted.

If modellers approach the philosophical literature on models with the goal of figuring out what models are and what a good model is, they might easily find themselves lured into naive monistic views of models that fail to represent the full epistemic richness of modelling practices, thereby turning them into worse scientists than they could have otherwise been.

It has been revealed that this could happen in several ways. For instance, models with epistemic functions not recognised by narrow monist accounts might be discarded. Consider, for example, models with weak predictive power, but great generality and insight into complex systems.

Sources indicate that perhaps Maynard Smith's worry is most strongly illustrated in economics, where Milton Friedman and Karl Popper are taken to have the "last word" in any methodological debate, and are frequently invoked to both defend and criticise the work of modellers. They are perhaps paradigm cases of monist thinking. Friedman argued that the only relevant desideratum in science concerns predictive power, while Popper argued that what matters is falsifiability.

According to recent reports, these accounts of science have received extensive criticism over the last decades. Indeed, the philosopher Alex Rosenberg argued that Friedman's naive picture single-handedly justified the existence of philosophy of economics as a distinct profession. Economists, however, are unlikely to read much if any work on methodology beyond Friedman and Popper. As the economist Dani Rodrik notes, economic methodology is relegated to specialised journals and, more importantly, is not really being taught in graduate school.

The result is that economists seem to believe that their science operates according to a simple form of falsificationism, a picture of science that, most contemporary philosophers of science would agree, both misrepresents scientific practice and provides the wrong ideal of how science ought to function.

The obvious counter to Maynard Smith's concern is that it is not an argument against the philosophy of science, but rather against bad philosophy of science, which limits, rather than fosters, insights into the richness of the epistemic tools available to scientists.

Recent findings suggest that philosophers are not innocent here. Some debates in the philosophy of science rest on such monist motivations to seek univocal accounts of laws, explanation, species, functions, preferences, and many more. As Peter Godfrey-Smith emphasised, one of the hazards of philosophy is the temptation to come up with theories that are "too broad and sweeping". This hazard has not been avoided in the philosophical literature on models. Many philosophers of science seem to be under the impression that once we figure out what "models" are and how they work, we can finally get a handle on all the other pressing questions in the philosophy of science. I argue that this way of thinking about models is grounded in a mistake.

Recent findings suggest that A philosophy of science worth reading takes the plurality, diversity, and richness of models and modelling practices seriously. It does not hand scientists a single criterion for good science.

Sources indicate that economists, Rodrik argues, need a better story about the kind of science they practise, and some economists have recently engaged with philosophical questions themselves, seeking contact with philosophers of economics in the process. Philosophers of science, in turn, should turn more of their attention toward both the social sciences and the philosophy of the social sciences. Their lack of engagement with this rich literature is a historical omission that may have provided a misguided understanding of how science works.

According to recent reports, should scientists ignore philosophers? They should ignore those who tell them that there is only one way of doing science well.

Godfrey-Smith, P. (2003). Theory and Reality: An Introduction to the Philosophy of Science. University of Chicago Press.

According to recent reports, maynard Smith, J. (1997). Interview by Richard Dawkins. Web of Stories. https://www.webofstories.com/play/john.maynard.smith/99.

Popper, K. (1959). The Logic of Scientific Discovery. Routledge.

Rodrik, D. (2015). Economics Rules: Why Economics Works, When It Fails, and How to Tell the Difference. Oxford University Press.

Tech Report: Becky the basset hound helps rescuers find her missing human on a New York mountain

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (423 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Becky the basset hound is giving new meaning to the term “man’s best friend.” On November 12, she walked to the Whiteface Lodge, a ski resort in Lake Placid, New York.
  • Industry observers note that the team at Whiteface called the Upcoming York State Police (NYSP), who contacted the Department of Conservation (DEC) Forest Rangers for assistance with the search.
  • the next morning, a hunter who was searching just ahead of the group heard someone fall and scream.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Becky the basset hound is giving new meaning to the term “man’s best friend.” On November 12, she walked to the Whiteface Lodge, a ski resort in Lake Placid, New York. The hotel staff immediately recognized the dog, but not because of her sparkling personality or floppy ears. Becky’s owner has dementia, and the unnamed man has disappeared before.

Industry observers note that the team at Whiteface called the Upcoming York State Police (NYSP), who contacted the Department of Conservation (DEC) Forest Rangers for assistance with the search. Four NYSP officers and 14 Rangers used drones and another dog (a bloodhound) to search for the missing person. According to Charlie Foutch, the lead Ranger on the search, it was about 25 to 30 degrees Fahrenheit overnight.

At 10 a.m. the next morning, a hunter who was searching just ahead of the group heard someone fall and scream. He found the missing man off to the side of a trail in a draining area with open woods. Ranger Sabo arrived on the scene shortly after. The 69-year-old man was not wearing gloves or shoes, and was suffering from some frostbite on his feet and hands. He was still alert and talking.

According to recent reports, “We’re always looking for live people. That’s our goal is to find a live person,” said Fouch. “And a lot of people are really tough. This gentleman didn’t have shoes on when we found him in the morning or mittens or gloves, so he had been out there for some period of time at night. And he still did okay. Sometimes if you keep moving in that situation, you generate enough heat to do okay.”.

Due to his injuries and the location off the trail, a hoist was the safest and quickest way to get him to safety. Ranger Martin used a cable to hoist him up to a helicopter, while NYSP Pilot Engle flew them to the hospital.

In addition to this coordination between hunters, the NYSP, and DEC, Fouch mentioned that Becky the basset hound made this happy ending possible.

“I think if the dog had not shown up at Whiteface, that gentleman definitely would have had a different outcome,” remarked Fouch. “It definitely would have been much harder to find him. He may not have survived the rest of the day and probably not another night. The dog definitely contributed to him being saved so quickly.”.

#168551. Juiced Scrambler Mini rolled out as a cooler (and safer) e-bike option for teens and parents

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1026 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

Juiced Scrambler Mini rolled out as a cooler (and safer) e-bike option for teens and parents

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1026 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Finding an electric bike for a teenager can be surprisingly tricky.
  • The newly released Juiced Scrambler Mini looks like it could do a pretty good job of threading that needle.
  • Recent findings suggest that the upcoming youth-sized e-bike takes the mini-motorcycle styling of Juiced’s larger Scrambler models and shrinks it down around 16-inch fat tires, creating a bike designed for riders between 4’0″ and 5’3″ (122 to 160 cm).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Finding an electric bike for a teenager can be surprisingly tricky. Parents generally want something safe, manageable, and from a reputable organization. Teenagers, meanwhile, generally want something that doesn’t look like it was picked out by their parents.

The newly released Juiced Scrambler Mini looks like it could do a pretty good job of threading that needle.

Recent findings suggest that the upcoming youth-sized e-bike takes the mini-motorcycle styling of Juiced’s larger Scrambler models and shrinks it down around 16-inch fat tires, creating a bike designed for riders between 4’0″ and 5’3″ (122 to 160 cm). But perhaps more importantly for parents, Juiced also built in a PIN-protected speed limiter known as Speed Lock that lets adults decide just how fast the bike can go.

Industry observers note that the Scrambler Mini ships set to a 10 mph (16 km/h) Beginner Mode, but its maximum speed can be adjusted anywhere from 1-20 mph (32 km/h) and then locked behind a four-digit PIN. Juiced notes that riders aged 8-12 should not exceed 10 mph, while riders 13 and older can use the bike at speeds up to 20 mph, subject of course to local laws and regulations. In almost every state and jurisdiction though, the bike will fit Class 2 designation for street-legal riding and bike lane operation.

Industry observers note that that setup seems like a pretty smart way to approach youth e-bikes. Instead of buying a slow bike that a teenager may quickly outgrow – or handing them a much faster machine before a parent thinks they’re ready – the same bike can essentially grow with the rider (with speed titrated by a parent or guardian).

And from the kid’s perspective, it certainly doesn’t look like a safety-first children’s bike.

The Scrambler Mini gets the same sort of moto-inspired styling that has defined Juiced’s Scrambler lineup, including a long bench seat, dual-crown-style fork, chunky 16 x 4-inch tires, and several appropriately loud color options including Blackberry, Fruit Punch, Blueberry, and Pink Lemonade.

There’s some decent hardware underneath that styling, too. The rear hub motor is rated at 500W nominal and 1,092W peak with 80 Nm of torque. A removable 48V 10Ah battery using LG cells provides 480Wh of capacity, with Juiced claiming up to 40 miles (64 km) of range. Four levels of cadence-based pedal assist are included, as is a right-side thumb throttle.

The bike also features Talon hydraulic disc brakes with large 180mm rotors front and rear, 50mm of front suspension travel, an integrated backlit LCD, a headlight, and a rear taillight with brake-light functionality. The single-speed bike weighs 59 lb (26.8 kg), has a 27.15-inch seat height, and is rated for up to 275 lb (125 kg) of payload.

Those parts are far above what we normally see on e-bikes targeted towards teens, with most teen-focused e-bikes sporting cheaper components like mechanical brakes and rigid forks.

The Scrambler Mini is listed at $1,099, though Juiced is presently offering a Black Friday sale that drops the price by another $150 to just $949. The firm notes preorders are expected to begin shipping the week of December 7.

Industry observers note that that price also comes with something increasingly important in the crowded youth e-bike market: an actual company standing behind the bike. Juiced was founded in 2009, swiftly becoming a leader in the market for powerful and stylish e-bikes. But after the brand’s financial troubles a few years ago, Lectric eBikes stepped in to take Juiced under its wing in 2025. The relaunched Juiced now offers a three-year manufacturer warranty and US-based support, plus the peace of mind that comes with backing from North America’s largest e-bike company, Lectric eBikes.

That last part may be just as appealing to parents as the speed limiter, though the 3-year warranty is definitely a deal sweetener, too.

Sources indicate that there’s always going to be some controversy around the idea of e-bikes marketed towards teens, but I’m for it when done responsibly. Let’s face it: e-bikes are incredibly popular and teens are already going to be riding them, even if it means borrowing a friend’s e-bike because they don’t have their own. So if they’re going to be riding, the least we can do is put them on a safer, higher-quality bike so they learn the right skills in the right environment. And hey, it sure beats teens sitting alone in their rooms texting each other all afternoon.

When it comes to choosing an e-bike, there are already plenty of cheap mini e-bikes and electric dirt bike-style machines floating around online, and many are undoubtedly going to look tempting to teenagers. The Scrambler Mini seems to take a different approach, giving young riders the styling, fat tires, throttle, and mini-moto attitude they actually want, while giving parents control over how much of that performance they can access.

It’s still an e-bike capable of 20 mph, and that means parents need to make decisions about where, when, and how their kids ride it. And there’s even an argument to be made for removing the throttle and turning it into a Class 1 e-bike in the beginning, requiring a teen to pedal it to engage the motor. But I’d much rather see that conversation happening around a bike with hydraulic brakes, lights, a programmable speed limit, and a real tech giant standing behind it than around some anonymous electric mini-bike bought from the depths of the internet.

And if the teenager thinks it looks cool enough to actually ride, that’s probably the point.
